title: Synthesis & Improvisation
hook: Improvisation is not abandoning the method; it is the method running so deep that you can feel when a moment needs something it never covered.
why:
No method covers everything. Sooner or later you will meet a moment that nothing in this book prepared you for: a laugh at a funeral, a stranger collapsing in grief on a train, a culture you have never seen, a friend's crisis that arrives in the middle of a celebration. In those moments the protocol can become a trap. You reach for a step that does not fit, or follow a rule whose reason has vanished, because following it feels safer than thinking.

This chapter is about what happens when the method meets something it did not anticipate. The research on expertise distinguishes experts who are fast at familiar problems from experts who can adapt to new ones, and shows how experienced people decide under pressure without weighing options. It explains why surprise is the most important signal you will ever get, when to break your own rules and how to know you are entitled to, and why improvising well with people means listening harder rather than performing better. It ends with the simplest tool of all, which is saying out loud that you do not know.

teach.p:
In 1986 the Japanese psychologists Giyoo Hatano and Kayoko Inagaki distinguished two courses that expertise can take. Routine experts become fast and accurate at the problems they meet often. Adaptive experts become just as good at familiar problems, but they also understand why their procedures work, and that understanding lets them modify the procedures, or invent new ones, when a problem arrives that the procedures do not fit.

The difference does not show on an ordinary day. A routine expert and an adaptive expert reading their own team in their own office look the same. Both know the baselines, both catch the changes, both make well-calibrated predictions. The difference shows when the situation changes in a way neither has met: a new team from another culture, a crisis, a person whose behaviour fits none of the patterns. The routine expert keeps applying procedures that no longer fit. The adaptive expert notices that they no longer fit, and knows enough about why they ever worked to build something that will.

Hatano and Inagaki suggested that adaptive expertise grows in particular conditions: when people meet varied problems rather than the same one repeatedly, when they are not under such pressure to perform that they only ever reach for what has worked before, and when they are encouraged to understand rather than only to succeed.

Much of this book has been an attempt to build the second kind. That is why every reading came with its disconfirming condition and every chapter with its research. A reader who knows only that the protocol says *start with a baseline* is a routine expert. A reader who knows why, that individual differences swamp universal meanings, can work out what to do when no baseline exists.

Understanding why is what lets you change how.
teach.disconfirm: If, faced with situations your procedures do not cover, you find you can adapt them as well without knowing the reasons behind them as with, understanding is not what drives your adaptability. Test it by explaining the reasons for three of your rules before the next unfamiliar situation, and compare.

teach.p:
In the 1980s Gary Klein and his colleagues set out to study how experienced fire commanders choose between options under pressure. They found that, for most of the decisions the commanders described, there was no choice between options at all. The commanders recognised the situation as a kind they had seen before, and that recognition brought with it a sense of what to expect, which cues mattered, what the goals were and what a typical response would be. They took the first workable response that came to mind and tested it by imagining it play out. If it seemed to work, they acted. If not, they adjusted it or tried the next.

Klein called this the recognition-primed decision model. It describes what the six steps of your protocol look like after years of use. You no longer run through them in order. You walk into a room and recognise that the man by the window is not bored but cornered, because the cluster, the timing and his baseline arrive together as a single impression. Then you imagine what would happen if you asked him directly, and you see him close up, so you try something gentler instead.

This is how the method is meant to end up: absorbed so deeply that it shows up as recognition rather than procedure. It is also why recognition can be trusted only as far as the experience behind it. Klein's commanders had seen hundreds of fires, with clear feedback. Your recognition is as good as your ledger says it is in that kind of situation, and no better.

When recognition comes quickly in a situation your ledger has never scored, treat it as a first guess, not a conclusion.
teach.disconfirm: If your quick recognitions in familiar situations turn out, when scored, to be no more accurate than readings you work through step by step, recognition has not yet absorbed the method. Keep working the steps until the ledger shows the difference.

teach.h: Run it forward in your head.
teach.p:
The second half of Klein's model is mental simulation. Before acting, the experienced commander imagines the action unfolding: if we go in through the front, the floor will hold for about this long, the crew will be here, the fire will move there. If the story runs smoothly, he acts. If it snags, the snag tells him what to change.

You can do the same with people, and it takes seconds. Before you say the sentence you are about to say, imagine the next thirty seconds. *If I say "you seem upset", he'll say "I'm fine" and turn away.* That snag suggests a better opening: a question about the situation, or simply sitting down beside him. *If I tell her what I noticed in the meeting now, with her colleague standing there, she'll be embarrassed.* That snag suggests waiting.

Simulation draws on everything you have recorded. The more scored predictions you have about how people respond to particular approaches, the more realistic your simulations become, and the more likely they are to snag in the right places. A simulation built on wishful thinking runs smoothly every time, which is why its smoothness should make you suspicious.

The most useful thing simulation does is to make you notice when you cannot simulate at all. If you try to imagine how a person will respond and nothing comes, or several very different outcomes seem equally likely, you are in a situation your experience does not cover. That is precisely the moment to slow down rather than act.

The story you can't tell yourself is the one you should ask them to tell you.
teach.disconfirm: If your mental simulations of how people will respond are no better than chance when you check them against what happens, they are built on hope rather than experience. Score a dozen of them in the ledger before relying on the technique.

teach.h: Surprise means the map has run out.
teach.p:
In Klein's model, recognition brings expectancies: things that should happen if the situation is what you think it is. When they are violated, the situation is not what you thought. Surprise is the most valuable signal you will ever get, because it is the only one that tells you directly that your reading is wrong.

The organisational theorist Karl Weick wrote about what can happen when surprise is not heeded. In 1949, at Mann Gulch in Montana, a crew of smokejumpers parachuted in to fight what looked like a routine fire. It was not. The fire crossed the gulch and raced uphill towards them. The crew's foreman, Wagner Dodge, did something no one had trained for: he lit a fire in the grass ahead of him and lay down in its ashes, and called for the others to join him. They did not understand, and ran on. Thirteen men died. Dodge survived, as did two others who found a gap in the rocks. Weick described it as a collapse of sensemaking. The crew's picture of the situation broke down faster than they could build a new one, and when one man improvised, the others could not follow, partly because he had no time to explain.

Most of your surprises will be smaller, but the shape is the same. A widower laughs through the eulogy. A man you expected to be angry is grateful. A colleague who should be relieved goes pale. At that moment the temptation is to force the surprise back into the old reading: he must be in shock, he must be pretending. Resist it.

When you are surprised, slow down, watch more widely, and treat your current picture of the situation as provisional. The protocol's steps still apply. Your recognition does not.
teach.disconfirm: If, when you look back through your journal, the moments you were surprised by someone turn out no more often than other moments to be the ones where your reading was wrong, surprise is not a useful signal for you. Most readers find the opposite, so count before deciding.
teach.pullQuote: Surprise is the only signal that tells you directly that your reading is wrong.

teach.h: When to break your own rules.
teach.p:
Every rule in this book exists for a reason. Ask before acting on a reading, because readings are guesses. Do not read people who are grieving, because they need presence rather than assessment. Describe before predicting in an unfamiliar culture, because your baseline is wrong there. Never test a reading by provoking someone, because it harms them and corrupts the evidence.

Adaptive expertise means knowing the reasons well enough to see when a case defeats them. A grieving friend who has stopped eating and speaks about not wanting to be here has moved from a moment for presence to a moment for acting, and the rule against reading him gives way to the duty to ask directly about suicide and help him reach support. A stranger collapsing in a culture you do not know needs help before he needs you to build a local baseline.

The test for breaking a rule has two parts, and you need both. First, can you say in one sentence why the rule exists? Second, can you say why this particular case defeats that reason? If you can answer both, you may be right to break it. If you can answer neither, or only the second, you are probably breaking it because it is inconvenient, or because you feel strongly, and feelings are what the rules were built to restrain.

One rule never breaks: the ethical floor. No case defeats the reasons against manipulation, against provoking people to test a reading, or against diagnosing someone from their body.

And whenever you do break a rule, write it up afterwards: the rule, the reason, why the case defeated it, and what happened. That entry is how your protocol learns the exception.
teach.disconfirm: If the rules you break by this test turn out, when you review the journal entries, to have been broken wrongly as often as rightly, the test is not working for you. Raise the bar by asking someone you trust to hear your two sentences before you act, where time allows.

teach.h: Improvise with a person, not at him.
teach.p:
Improvisation in the arts is often misunderstood as invention from nothing. The people who do it best describe something different. In his study of jazz, *Thinking in Jazz*, the ethnomusicologist Paul Berliner showed how improvising musicians spend years absorbing a vocabulary of phrases, tunes and harmonic moves, by listening, copying and practising, so that in performance they can respond to what the other players do. Improvisation is a conversation, and it rests on a large store of absorbed material.

In theatre, Keith Johnstone's book *Impro* described the improviser's basic discipline in terms of offers. Everything the other actor does or says is an offer. A good improviser accepts it and builds on it. A poor one blocks it, ignoring or overriding what was offered in order to carry on with his own idea.

When you improvise with a person, the same holds. The moment calls for something the method did not cover, and the temptation is to fill the gap with a clever move of your own. Usually the better move is to treat what the other person is doing as an offer. If a grieving man starts telling a funny story about his father, follow the story and laugh. If a frightened teenager will talk only about a video game, talk about the game. If a colleague in crisis wants to do something practical rather than talk, do the practical thing beside him.

Your absorbed vocabulary, the baselines, the clusters, the ledger, is what lets you hear the offer. Your job in the moment is not to show what you know. It is to respond to what you are given.
teach.disconfirm: If following the other person's lead in unscripted moments regularly leaves them more distressed or the situation less safe than your own plan would have, you are accepting offers that should have been declined. Keep safety and the ethical floor above any offer.

teach.p:
When the method has run out, the most useful thing you can say is often the simplest: *I'm not sure what's happening here. Can you tell me?* It is also one of the hardest sentences for many men to say, because it sounds like weakness. In practice it does the opposite.

In 2017 Mark Leary and colleagues studied intellectual humility, the recognition that one's beliefs might be wrong. People higher in it were better at telling strong arguments from weak ones, and judged others who changed their minds less harshly. Humility is not a lack of knowledge. It is an accurate sense of where your knowledge ends, which is exactly what calibration has been training.

Saying that you do not know does three things at once. It tells the other person that you are not reading them from behind a wall of certainty. It invites them to become the authority on their own situation, which they are. And it buys you time to build a new picture when the old one has failed.

It also does what Wagner Dodge had no time to do at Mann Gulch: it lets others follow your improvisation. When you depart from what people expect of you, say what you are doing and why, in a sentence. *I'm going to sit here quietly with him for a bit rather than call anyone yet.* *I'm going to stop the meeting for five minutes.* People follow an improvisation they understand.

The reader who has mastered the method is not the one who always knows. He is the one who knows exactly when he does not, and says so.
teach.disconfirm: If saying plainly that you do not know what is happening makes people trust you less, over several such moments in a particular setting, that setting may punish uncertainty in a way most do not. Check whether the problem is the admission itself or the absence of a next step alongside it.

poseGallery.doCaption: Slowing down to work out what the situation now is.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Holding on to the old reading when the situation has changed.
poseGallery.annotation: Surprise is the signal that your map has run out. Forcing the surprise into the old reading is how sensemaking collapses.

poseGallery.doCaption: Treating what he does as an offer, and building on it.
poseGallery.annotation: Improvisation is a conversation. The absorbed method is what lets you hear the offer; the moment asks you to respond to it.

poseGallery.doCaption: Saying: I'm not sure what's happening here. Can you tell me?
poseGallery.annotation: Admitting where your knowledge ends makes the other person the authority on their own situation, and lets others follow you.

poseGallery.doCaption: Breaking it because you can say why this case defeats its reason.
poseGallery.dontCaption: Breaking a rule because it is inconvenient.
poseGallery.annotation: A rule may be broken when you can name its reason and why the case defeats it. The ethical floor never breaks.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Steering him to talk about it, face to face

caseStudy:
Gareth, fifty-eight, has been a funeral director for thirty years. His rules are simple and he has taught them to every new member of staff: be present, be quiet, never read the mourners, never approach anyone uninvited.

At a funeral in November the widower laughs loudly, twice, during the eulogy. One of Gareth's younger staff moves towards him, ready to guide him out. Gareth stops her with a hand. He is surprised, and he knows that surprise means his picture is wrong. So he slows down and watches more widely. The widow's sister is smiling. So are the grandchildren. The minister pauses and says, warmly, that Derek had asked for exactly this: no solemn faces, and the story about the caravan. The laughter is the offer, and the room has accepted it. Gareth lets it be.

After the service, at the back of the hall, he sees the dead man's son standing alone. He is perhaps twenty, very still, and shaking, with his car keys in his hand. He has not spoken to anyone. Gareth's rule says do not approach. He asks himself why the rule exists, to protect people from intrusion when they need to be left alone, and whether this case defeats it. The keys and the shaking say this young man is about to drive, and may not be safe to.

So he breaks the rule, and says what he is doing. *I don't know what you need, and you can tell me to go away. I didn't want you to be on your own. Will you sit for a minute and have a cup of tea before you drive?* The young man sits. After a while he says he cannot remember the way home. Gareth finds his cousin, who drives him.

That evening Gareth writes the exception in the notebook he keeps for new staff, with the rule, the reason, and why this case defeated it.
observe: Notice one moment this week when a person's behaviour surprised you, and what you did in the ten seconds that followed.
Watch someone highly skilled respond to something unexpected in their work, in person or on video, and notice what they kept and what they changed.
Notice one rule you follow with people, and check whether you can say the reason for it in a single sentence.

drills.name: Rule Reasons
steps: List ten rules you follow when reading people, from your protocol and from this book.
Next to each, write in one sentence why it exists.
Mark any rule whose reason you could not write, and go back to the chapter it came from.
For five of the rules, write one case in which the reason would not apply.
For each of those cases, write what you would do instead, and mark any that would cross the ethical floor.
variations: Ask a friend to choose five of your rules and say why they think each exists, then compare their reasons with yours.
For each rule, write the earliest moment in your journal when you would have broken it if you had known what you know now.
Repeat the drill with rules you were taught at work, and see how many of their reasons you can state.

drills.name: Run It Forward
steps: Before three conversations this week, choose the first thing you intend to say.
Imagine the thirty seconds that follow, as specifically as you can.
Note where the imagined conversation snags, and change your opening to avoid the snag.
After each conversation, write whether the snag you foresaw appeared.
Score your simulations in the ledger like any other prediction.
variations: Simulate two versions before each conversation, the one you hope for and the one you fear, and note which was closer.
Run a simulation for a conversation with someone you know very well and for a stranger, and compare how often each snags.
Ask the other person afterwards, where it is natural, what they had expected you to say, and compare it with your simulation.

drills.name: Surprise Log
steps: For a week, write down every moment when someone's behaviour surprised you.
For each, note what you had expected and why.
Note what you did next: forced the surprise into your old reading, or slowed down and looked again.
Where you found out more later, note which response served you better.
At the end of the week, write one sentence about how you usually respond to surprise.
variations: Add a column for your body's response to each surprise, such as a jolt in the chest or a flash of irritation, and look for a pattern.
Log surprises from films and television as well as life, and see whether you respond to them differently.
At the end of a second week, compare the two weeks and note whether you are forcing fewer surprises into old readings.

drills.name: Accept the Offer
steps: With a friend, agree a stop word and a simple setting, such as two strangers waiting for a delayed train.
For three minutes, improvise a conversation in which every reply must accept and build on what the other person just said or did.
Ask your friend to introduce an unexpected emotional turn, such as sudden bad news, without warning you.
Respond to what they offer rather than to what you had planned.
Talk afterwards about the moments when you blocked an offer, and what you could have done instead.
variations: Repeat the exercise with the roles reversed, so that you are the one who introduces the unexpected turn.
Try a version in which neither of you may speak, and offers must be made only with posture, gesture and movement.
Run it in a setting closer to your work, such as a customer or a colleague, and note which of your work habits block offers.

drills.name: Novel Case Rehearsal
steps: Choose a situation with a person that you have never faced, such as someone collapsing in grief in a public place or a colleague's panic attack.
Write what you would expect to see, and what would surprise you.
List which of your rules would hold and which might need to break, with the reason in each case.
Write the sentence you would use to say that you do not know what is needed.
Say it aloud three times, and write down what you would do in the first minute.
variations: Rehearse a case with a friend playing the other person, and ask them afterwards which of your first-minute actions helped.
Choose a case that involves a child or an older person, and note which rules change and why.
Read the relevant chapter of this book after you have written your plan, and note what you would now add or remove.

quiz.q: What does improvising mean, for a reader of people who has absorbed the method?
options: Dropping the method and trusting whatever your instincts say in the moment
Adapting the absorbed method to a moment it never covered
Using whichever technique seems most likely to get you a result quickly
Following the protocol even more strictly than usual when things get strange
quiz.explain: Improvisation rests on the method rather than replacing it. Knowing why each step exists is what lets you change it when a moment needs something the steps never anticipated.

quiz.q: According to Hatano and Inagaki, what distinguishes adaptive experts from routine experts?
options: They understand why their procedures work, so they can change them
They are faster and more accurate on the familiar problems they meet often
They have spent more years in their field than routine experts usually have
They rely on intuition alone and avoid using procedures of any kind at all
quiz.explain: Both kinds of expert can be excellent on familiar problems. The adaptive expert's understanding of why procedures work is what lets them modify or invent procedures when a problem arrives that the usual ones do not fit.

quiz.q: What did Gary Klein find about how experienced fire commanders made most of their decisions?
options: They compared several options carefully before choosing between them
They followed the written procedure exactly in every situation they met
They chose more or less at random and justified the choice afterwards
They recognised the situation and tested one response in their heads
quiz.explain: Recognition brought expectations and a typical response, which they checked by imagining it play out. This is what a well-absorbed method looks like, and why it can only be trusted as far as the experience behind it.

quiz.q: At a wedding, the groom's father weeps through the speeches while everyone around him laughs. You had expected joy. What fits this chapter?
options: Read it as grief, and go over to comfort him straight away
Ignore it, since weddings make everyone a little emotional
Take the surprise as a sign to slow down and look more widely
Ask the people sitting near him what is wrong with him today
quiz.explain: Surprise tells you that your picture is wrong, but not what the right one is. Slowing down and watching more widely keeps you from forcing it into a new story too quickly. If you are close to him, a gentle question later can follow.

quiz.q: What does Karl Weick's account of the Mann Gulch fire suggest about improvising under pressure?
options: That improvising is always more dangerous than following the rules
That an improvisation others cannot understand may not be followed
That experienced leaders should never depart from their training
That crews in a crisis should always split up and act independently
quiz.explain: Dodge's escape fire saved his life, but his crew did not understand it and ran on. When you depart from what others expect, say what you are doing and why, so that they can follow.

quiz.q: Your rule is never to approach mourners uninvited. After a funeral, a young man stands alone, shaking, with his car keys in his hand. What fits?
options: Keep to the rule, since it exists to protect people who are grieving from intrusion
Approach him, since any rule can be broken when you feel strongly enough about it
Leave it to his family, since it is their place to notice and deal with him
Break it, since you can name a safety reason, and say plainly what you are doing
quiz.explain: You can say why the rule exists and why this case defeats it: he may be about to drive when he is not safe to. Breaking it openly, with a simple offer he can refuse, respects both his grief and his safety.

quiz.q: What did Paul Berliner's study of jazz musicians show about improvisation?
options: That good improvisers invent everything on the spot, and avoid learning other musicians' phrases
That improvisation is a gift some musicians are born with, and practice does little to develop it
That improvising musicians spend years absorbing a vocabulary, which lets them respond to the others
That most jazz solos are written out in advance and only made to sound as if they were improvised
quiz.explain: Improvisation rests on a large store of absorbed material, built by listening, copying and practising. For a reader of people, the absorbed vocabulary of baselines, clusters and the ledger is what lets you hear the other person's offer.

quiz.q: A month after his wife moved out, you visit a friend who wants only to fix his bike, and changes the subject every time you ask how he is. What fits this chapter?
options: Pick up a spanner and help with the bike, and let him say what he wants to, when he is ready
Insist on talking about his feelings, since avoiding them now will only make things worse later
Leave, since he has made it clear that he does not want your company or your help at all
Tell him plainly that he is in denial, so that he understands why you have come round to see him
quiz.explain: Everything the other person does is an offer. Fixing the bike is a way of being together without having to talk face to face, and side by side, with something to do, many people find it easier to say what is hard.

quiz.q: Someone says that admitting you do not know makes you look weak and less competent. What did Leary and colleagues find in 2017?
options: That people high in intellectual humility were seen as weak by others, and were trusted much less as a result
That intellectual humility made no measurable difference to how people judged arguments
That intellectually humble people simply knew less than everyone else, which is why they admitted it so often
That people higher in it told strong arguments from weak ones better and judged mind-changers less harshly
quiz.explain: Intellectual humility is an accurate sense of where your knowledge ends, which is what calibration trains. Saying that you do not know makes the other person the authority on their own situation and lets others follow your improvisation.

reflection.prompt: Describe one specific moment when a situation with a person went beyond anything your usual approach covered: a surprise, a crisis, a culture you did not know, a grief you had not met before. What did you do in the first minute? Which of your usual rules did you keep, and which did you set aside? Looking back, could you have said at the time why each rule did or did not fit, and what would you want to do the next time something similar happens?
reflection.guidance: The point is not to judge whether you got it right, but to see how you behave when the map runs out. Some people freeze and cling to the familiar steps; others abandon everything and act on feeling. Notice which you did. If you set a rule aside, try writing the two sentences now: why the rule exists, and why the case defeated it.

failureMode: The first failure is to use improvisation as an excuse, calling it adaptive expertise when it is really a return to unchecked instinct and an abandoned ledger. The second is the opposite: clinging to the protocol when the situation has plainly changed, and forcing every surprise back into the old reading. The third is breaking rules on feeling rather than reason, and calling the feeling judgment. The fourth is improvising alone, without saying what you are doing, so that the people around you cannot follow or help. The last is failing to write the exception down afterwards, which means the protocol never learns it and the next person you teach never hears of it.

moreCases.title: The teacher whose pupil laughed at bad news
moreCases.scene:
Amira, thirty-four, teaches a Year 9 class. On a Monday morning the head of year asks her to tell the class that their friend Leon was in a serious car accident at the weekend, that he is in hospital and is expected to recover, and that the school will share news when it can. Amira prepares what she will say, and says it gently.

As she finishes, Kyle, fourteen, at the back of the room, laughs: a short, loud burst that he tries to stop and cannot. Several pupils turn to stare at him. Amira feels a flash of anger. Her rule, built over ten years, is that disrespect in the classroom is dealt with at once and in front of the class, because letting it go teaches everyone that it is allowed. She tells Kyle that his behaviour is disgusting and sends him to wait outside.

At break she finds him sitting on the floor in the corridor, white-faced. He tells her that Leon is his best friend, that they were meant to be in the car together, and that he does not know why he laughed. He has been laughing at things all weekend and cannot make it stop.

Amira sits down on the floor next to him.

Several of the class had been laughing nervously at small things all morning, she realises later, and she had told two of them to settle down.

The head of year had warned her that some of Leon's friends might take the news badly. She had pictured tears, not laughter.
moreCases.misread:
Amira read Kyle's laugh through her strongest classroom rule, as disrespect, without noticing that it surprised her. The surprise was the signal that her picture was wrong, and she forced it back into the old reading instead.

She also read the class's stares at Kyle as agreement with her judgement, when most of them were frightened by the laugh and by the news together.
moreCases.betterRead:
Laughter at terrible news is not unusual, and it often comes from shock rather than contempt. But Amira did not need to know that to read the moment better. She needed to notice the surprise. A laugh from a pupil who is not normally cruel, at news about his own friend, does not fit the pattern her rule was built for, and an unexpected behaviour is the moment to slow down and watch more widely. The rule's reason, that open disrespect should not be allowed to stand, was defeated by a case she had not yet understood. A quiet *Kyle, are you all right? Come and see me in a minute* would have kept the room safe and left the reading open.

Amira later apologised to Kyle, with his parents present, and wrote the exception into her own notes.

The rule itself survived. What changed was that Amira added a line to her notes: when a behaviour surprises you, find out what it is before you decide what it means.

moreCases.title: The interviewer who stuck to the script
moreCases.scene:
Jane, fifty, chairs interview panels for a housing charity and is proud of how fair they are. Every candidate is asked the same questions in the same order, and the panel does not chat or go off script, because that is how bias creeps in.

The fourth candidate of the day, Bronwen, forty-two, is applying for a support worker role. She answers the first questions well. When Jane asks her, as she asks everyone, to explain the two-year gap in her employment history, Bronwen says that her husband was ill and died, and that she cared for him. Then she starts to cry, and cannot stop.

Jane waits a moment, then moves on to the next question, about handling a difficult tenant, in the same even voice. Bronwen tries to answer through her tears and loses her thread. The panel's scores for that question are low. Jane asks the remaining questions in order. At the end she thanks Bronwen and tells her they will be in touch.

Afterwards one of the other panel members, Tom, says that he felt terrible. Jane says she did too, but that pausing for one candidate and not for others would have been unfair.

Jane had once chaired a panel that was later criticised for favouring a candidate the members liked, and she had built her rules carefully after it.
moreCases.misread:
Jane read her rule as requiring her to carry on, because the rule was about treating everyone identically. She read sticking to the script as fairness, when in that moment it was producing a score that measured grief rather than ability.

She also read her own discomfort as a sign that she was being properly impartial, as if fairness should always feel bad.
moreCases.betterRead:
The rule test has two parts. Why does the rule exist? To make sure every candidate is judged on the same questions, without the panel's feelings tilting the result. Does this case defeat that reason? Pausing would not have changed the questions or how answers were scored. It would only have let the candidate answer them, which is what the rule was for. A better response was within the rule's spirit: *Let's take a few minutes. There's water here, and there's no hurry.* If Bronwen could not continue, the panel could offer to finish another day. Jane wrote to Bronwen the next morning and offered her a second interview, which Bronwen accepted.

Bronwen was appointed. She told Jane later that the second interview had been the first time anyone had asked her about her caring without flinching.

moreCases.title: The friend who blocked the offer
moreCases.scene:
Leo, thirty-three, drives over to see his friend Matt, thirty-four, a month after Matt's wife moved out. Leo has read the chapters on grief and on friendship, and has a plan: get Matt to open up. He arrives with beer and a speech prepared about how it is all right not to be all right.

Matt meets him at the door with oil on his hands and says he is fixing the gears on his bike. Leo says the bike can wait and that he wants to know how Matt really is. Matt says he is fine, and goes back to the bike. Leo follows him into the garage and asks how he is sleeping. Matt says fine. Leo asks whether he has talked to anyone. Matt says he is talking to Leo, isn't he, and turns the bike upside down.

For an hour Leo keeps steering back to feelings, and Matt keeps steering back to the bike. Leo leaves feeling that Matt has shut him out, and tells his partner that Matt is in denial.

Two days later Matt's brother texts Leo to say that Matt had told him Leo came round and that it was nice of him, but that he had just wanted some help with the bike.

Leo had been through a divorce himself three years earlier, and remembered wanting someone to make him talk about it. He had assumed Matt would want the same.
moreCases.misread:
Leo read Matt's bike as avoidance, a block to the conversation that mattered. Matt was offering the only kind of conversation he could manage that day, and Leo blocked the offer to carry on with his own plan.

He also read his own experience as Matt's, and his own plan as what Matt needed, without checking either.

And he read *I'm talking to you, aren't I?* as a brush-off, when it was close to the most Matt could say that day.
moreCases.betterRead:
Keith Johnstone's discipline for improvisers applies: everything the other person does is an offer, and the good improviser accepts it and builds on it rather than blocking it to pursue his own idea. A man fixing a bike a month after his wife left is offering a way to be together without having to talk face to face. Leo's better move was to pick up a spanner. Side by side, with something to do with their hands, many people find it far easier to say a little about what is hard, and they say it when they are ready. A week later Leo went back, helped with the brakes, and said nothing about feelings. Halfway through, Matt said he had not been sleeping much.

Leo told his partner afterwards that the hardest part was not asking, and that he had never felt so useful.

moreCases.title: The father who said he did not know
moreCases.scene:
Paul, forty-four, has spent a year working through this book, and he reads his daughter Ellie, fourteen, well. He knows her baselines, her silences, the way she goes quiet when she is worried about school and loud when she is happy.

One evening Ellie comes home from her music lesson and does something he has never seen. She laughs and cries at the same time, sits on the stairs, and when he asks what is wrong she says *nothing*, and laughs again, and wipes her eyes. Paul runs through everything he knows and none of it fits. Her baseline offers no match. His recognition offers nothing at all. He tries to imagine what would happen if he asked her straight out what had happened, and he cannot picture her answer.

Paul notices that he cannot simulate the next minute, and remembers what that means. He sits down on the stair below her and says, *I don't know what's going on, and you don't have to tell me now. I'm here, and I'm not going anywhere.*

After a few minutes Ellie shows him an email on her phone. She has been offered a place at a specialist music school two hundred miles away, which she applied for without telling anyone in case she failed.

Ellie had practised for the audition at her friend's house for two months, saying she was doing homework.
moreCases.misread:
Paul could have read the tears as distress and the laughter as covering it, and pressed her for the problem. That reading would have forced a surprise into an old pattern, and missed that she was overwhelmed by something she wanted and was afraid of.

The old reading would also have told him what to do: find the problem and fix it, which is what he always did when she cried.
moreCases.betterRead:
When recognition offers nothing and simulation cannot tell you what will happen next, you are in a situation your experience does not cover, and that is the moment to slow down rather than act. Saying *I don't know* did what Leary's work on intellectual humility suggests it can. It told Ellie that he was not reading her from behind certainty, and it made her the authority on her own situation, which she was. They talked until midnight about whether she should go: joy and fear in the same evening, and both of them real. In the end she went, and came home every other weekend.

Paul wrote in his journal that night that the most useful thing he had said in a year was that he did not know.

He also noticed that his reading of her had not been wrong, exactly: she was distressed. It was only that distress was half of it, and he could not have known which half mattered without asking.

workedReading.title: A stranger in tears on the train
workedReading.scene:
Nisha, thirty-seven, is on her evening train home when the man sitting opposite her, in his sixties and wearing a suit, takes a phone call, listens for a minute, says *thank you* and hangs up. Then he begins to cry, silently, staring out of the window, with his phone still in his hand. The carriage is half full. Nobody says anything. Nisha's protocol says that in public she reads situations rather than individuals, and that she does not approach strangers uninvited. Neither rule seems to fit what is happening in front of her. She has eleven minutes until her stop.

She does not know him and will almost certainly never see him again, which makes every rule she has feel both more and less important.

She has read about this kind of moment in the chapter and has never met one.

steps.label: Notice the recognition
steps.text:
Her recognition arrives at once, as a single impression: bad news, grief or shock, and a man trying not to be seen. She notes it as a first guess, not a conclusion, because her ledger has almost nothing in it about strangers on trains. She also notices her own body: a tightening in her chest and an urge to look away, which is what everyone else in the carriage seems to be doing.

She does not stare. She looks at him once, long enough to see the phone and the tears, and then looks at the window too.

She also notices that her recognition comes with an urge to fix things, and decides that fixing is not her job here.

steps.label: Run it forward
steps.text:
She imagines the next thirty seconds. *If I lean across and ask whether he's all right, in front of everyone, he'll be embarrassed and say he's fine, and turn further to the window.* That snag tells her to change the opening. *If I hold out a tissue without saying anything, he can take it or not, and nobody needs to look.* That version runs more smoothly, which makes her a little suspicious of it, but it asks almost nothing of him.

She also imagines doing nothing, and that version runs smoothly too. She notices that it is the one she would choose if she were only protecting herself.

steps.label: Check the rule's reason
steps.text:
She asks herself why her rule about strangers exists: to avoid intruding on people who have not invited her attention, and to avoid treating them as material. Does this case defeat it? Partly. The man has not invited anything. But he is alone and distressed, and a small offer that he can ignore respects his choice better than nothing does. The ethical floor is untouched. She decides that a tissue and one sentence are within the reason for the rule.

She also decides that if he does not take the tissues, she will put them on the seat beside him and leave it at that.

She is also clear about where the rule stops: she will not ask what happened, and if he turns away, she will leave him be.

steps.label: Make a small offer
steps.text:
She holds out a packet of tissues. He looks at it, then at her, and takes one. She says quietly, *I'm getting off in a few stops, but I'm here if you want anything.* He nods and wipes his eyes. For a minute nothing happens. Then he says that his wife has been in hospital for a week, and that the call was from the ward. She is stable, he says, but they do not know what happens next, and he has not told their children yet.

She does not ask questions. She lets him say as much as he wants to and no more.

The carriage is quiet around them. A woman across the aisle catches Nisha's eye briefly and looks away again, kindly.

steps.label: Accept what he offers
steps.text:
Nisha does not ask about the illness. After a pause, the man starts talking about their garden: his wife's roses, which he has been watering every evening, badly, he says. Nisha treats it as the offer it is and asks about the roses. He tells her about a climbing rose his wife planted when they moved in, thirty years ago. He almost laughs. Nisha listens. She does not give advice or try to make him feel better.

She notices that the garden is where he wants to be, and that talking about the roses lets him talk about his wife without talking about the hospital.

When he stops talking, she lets the silence sit. He seems more comfortable in it than he was before.

steps.label: Say what she doesn't know
steps.text:
At the stop before hers, she says, *I don't know what would help, but is there anyone you can ring tonight, so you're not on your own with it?* He says his son, and that he will. Nisha has also been watching, quietly, for any sign that he might be at risk, such as talk of not wanting to go on, which would have changed everything, and has seen none. She says goodbye and gets off.

If she had seen signs of risk, she would have asked him directly and stayed, and missed her stop. That was part of her plan from the start.

steps.label: Write the exception
steps.text:
That evening she writes a journal entry, as Gareth does for his staff: the rule, *in public, don't approach strangers uninvited*; its reason, *to avoid intrusion and treating people as material*; why this case partly defeated it, *alone, distressed, and the offer could be ignored*; and what happened. She adds a line to her protocol's public variant: *a small offer that can be ignored is allowed.*

She also notes that her recognition, bad news and grief, was roughly right, and that what she did with it mattered much more than whether it was right.

She also writes down how she felt afterwards, shaky and unsure whether she had done the right thing, because that too will be useful next time.

moreFailures.title: Trusting quick recognition in a new kind of situation
moreFailures.body:
Recognition feels the same whether it rests on hundreds of scored readings or on none. In a familiar setting, the instant sense that a colleague is cornered or a friend is not fine may be worth trusting, because your ledger says it usually is. In a setting you have never scored, such as a stranger's crisis, an unfamiliar culture or a kind of grief you have never met, the same instant sense arrives with the same confidence and very little behind it. Klein's commanders could trust their recognition because they had seen hundreds of fires with clear feedback. Ask, when an impression arrives quickly, whether you have ever been scored in this kind of situation. If not, treat it as a first guess, act on it only in ways that are safe if it is wrong, and look harder for the moment it fails.

It may help to keep a short list at the front of your journal of the kinds of situations your ledger has scored, so that you can see at a glance when you are outside them.

moreFailures.title: Simulating only the version you want
moreFailures.body:
Mental simulation is only useful if it can snag. When you imagine a conversation going exactly as you hope, with the other person responding to your opening just as you planned, the simulation has told you about your wishes rather than about them. This is especially common when you are keen to help, as Leo was with Matt, or when you have rehearsed a speech. A useful check is to simulate at least two versions: the one you hope for and the one you fear, and then ask which is more like what has happened before with this person. If your simulations never snag, build them from your ledger rather than your hopes: what did this person actually do the last three times someone tried this?

The fear version is useful even if it is unlikely, because it tells you what to watch for in the first seconds.

Another check is to simulate from the other person's point of view: what would they hope you will say, and what would they dread?

moreFailures.title: Explaining the improvisation at length
moreFailures.body:
Saying what you are doing when you depart from what people expect is important, because people follow an improvisation they understand. But the explanation should be a sentence, not a speech. In a moment that needs action, a long account of your reasoning takes attention from the person who needs it and can sound like self-justification. *I'm going to sit with him for a bit before we call anyone* is enough. *I'm stopping the meeting for five minutes* is enough. The full reasoning belongs afterwards, in the journal entry and, if needed, in a conversation with the people who were there. Dodge's tragedy at Mann Gulch was that he had no time for even one sentence. Most of the time you will have exactly enough for one.

If people need more explanation in the moment, they will ask. Answer briefly and go back to the person.

A related failure is to say nothing at all, out of a fear of sounding unsure. One plain sentence is almost always better than silence.

moreFailures.title: Accepting an offer that causes harm
moreFailures.body:
Treating what the other person does as an offer is a discipline for staying with them, not a rule that you must go along with anything. If a friend's offer is to drive home after drinking, the improvisation is to take his keys and find another way, kindly. If someone in distress talks about ending their life, the offer you accept is the conversation, not the plan: ask directly about suicide, stay with them and help them reach support, as chapter 2.13 sets out. If someone wants you to help them do something that would hurt another person, the ethical floor holds. Accept the person and their way of being in the moment. Decline anything that would harm them or someone else, and say so plainly.

Improvisation lives inside the ethical floor, never above it.

The test is whether accepting the offer would leave the person, or anyone else, worse off. If it would, the offer you accept is the person, not the plan.

questions.q: How can I tell whether I am adapting well or simply trusting my instincts again?
questions.a:
Three checks help. First, can you say why each of your rules exists? The rule reasons drill is a test of that, and an adaptive reader can answer most of it without looking anything up. Second, how do you respond to surprise? Your surprise log will show whether you usually slow down or force the surprise into your old reading. Third, do you write the exceptions down? An adaptive reader who breaks a rule can explain why afterwards, in a sentence, and records it. Someone simply trusting instinct breaks rules without noticing, rarely writes anything down, and feels certain throughout. If your ledger has stopped being kept, that alone tells you which you are doing.

A fourth check is simply to ask an honest mirror whether you have become more or less careful with people since you started this book.

A fifth check is how you feel when you are shown to be wrong. An adaptive reader is interested; someone trusting instinct is usually annoyed.

questions.q: Isn't accepting someone's offer just telling them what they want to hear?
questions.a:
No. Accepting an offer means taking what the other person is doing or saying as the starting point, rather than overriding it with your plan. It does not mean agreeing with their claims or pretending. If a grieving man tells a funny story, accepting the offer means listening and laughing, not agreeing that he is coping well. If a colleague in crisis wants to do something practical, accepting it means doing the practical thing beside her, not telling her that she is right not to talk about it. You can still be honest, still ask, and still decline anything harmful. What you give up is the urge to steer the person back to the conversation you had prepared.

The practical test is whether the person feels more heard after you have spoken. If they feel steered, you have blocked; if they feel flattered, you have stopped being honest.

It also helps to remember that offers include silences, a change of subject and a refusal. Accepting a refusal is often the most respectful thing you can do.

questions.q: What should I do if I improvise and it goes badly wrong?
questions.a:
What you would do after any mistake with a person. Apologise plainly and without excuses, if an apology is owed. Repair what you can, which often means asking the person what would help now. Then write it up honestly: what you expected, what surprised you, what you did, and why it went wrong. Most improvisations that respect the person and stay above the ethical floor can be recovered from, even when they misfire. A small offer that was not wanted is easily withdrawn. The ones that cannot be undone are those that cross the floor, such as manipulation or a diagnosis made from someone's body, which is one reason the floor never moves.

It is also worth asking yourself, honestly, whether doing nothing would have been better. Sometimes it would, and that too is worth knowing.

Write down, too, what the other person did that told you it had gone wrong, so that you can catch it sooner next time.

questions.q: Can I practise improvising with people when nothing real is at stake?
questions.a:
Yes, and you should, because it is much harder to learn for the first time when something real is at stake. The drills in this chapter are a start, especially accepting the offer with a friend and rehearsing a novel case. An improvisation class, of the kind many theatres and community centres run, is excellent practice in listening and building on offers, and most people find it more enjoyable than they expect. You can also practise on recordings: pause a film or a documentary at a moment the characters did not expect, and ask what you would have done, then see what happened. Score those predictions too.

If you take a class, notice which of your habits block offers most often, and add them to your stress signature or your protocol.

Practise with people you trust, and keep the stakes low, so that a misfire is a lesson rather than an injury.

questions.q: How do I explain to the people I work with when I break one of our own rules?
questions.a:
At the time, in one sentence: what you are doing, and if possible why. *I'm going to talk to him on his own before we go any further.* Later, when things are calm, explain more fully, using the two-part test: why the rule exists, and why this case defeated that reason. Invite people to challenge it. If they think you were wrong, they may be right, and the conversation will improve the rule either way. Then write the exception down where others can see it, as Gareth does for his staff, so that the next person who meets the same situation knows it has happened before and what was done.

The aim is not to defend the decision but to share what you learned, so that the team's rules grow from real cases.

Over a year, a team's written exceptions become one of its most valuable records, because they hold the cases that no rule foresaw.

questions.q: Is there a point at which I should stop using the method altogether?
questions.a:
Not altogether, but it changes. Over time, the six steps stop being steps and become the way you see, so you are using the method without running it. That is the point of this chapter. The parts that should never stop are the checks that keep you honest: a ledger, even a light one, so that your recognition stays calibrated; the habit of noticing surprise; and the ethical floor. What should stop, at the right times, is reading people at all. The last chapter, on the quiet body, is about that: when to take the skill off duty, so that you can simply be with the people you have spent this book learning to see.

By then, the method will mostly show itself in what you do not do: the reading you do not announce, the question you ask instead, and the moment you let pass.

It will also show in what you notice, which will be more than before, and in how lightly you hold it.

watch.title: Every Season Sixteen Scenes From A Hat
watch.notice: Improvisers build scenes with no script by reading each other moment to moment. Notice how they pick up each other's offers from posture, gaze and timing.

reviewPrompt: The next time someone surprises you, slow down for ten seconds and look more widely before forming any new reading of them.
